thread.title: How Spotify influences what songs become popular (or not)

author: Jacob Passy
title: How Spotify influences what songs become popular (or not)
text:
Published: June 18, 2018 2:38 p.m. ET Share
Getting on certain playlists can lead to a major windfall for musicians Getty Images Playlists are major drivers of listener traffic on streaming platforms like Spotify.
By Jacob Passy
While streaming platforms have opened up access to a much wider array of music for listeners, they still exercise a great deal of influence over what exactly consumers listen to.
On the surface, services like Spotify SPOT, -0.38% Pandora P, +2.89% and Apple Music AAPL, -0.05% have leveled the playing field for musicians seeking audiences by virtue of the sheer amount of music they provide access to. Looking at Spotify alone, the streaming service added roughly 1.5 million songs to its catalog in 2016 and 2017.
But the way that these streaming platforms suggest music to listeners has a major influence on their listening habits. And playlists in particular are instrumental in guiding consumers to specific content, according to a new working paper by researchers at the European Commission’s Joint Research Center and the University of Minnesota.
The researchers looked at data for the daily top 200 songs from Spotify over 2016 and 2017. The researchers chose Spotify in particular, because it had the largest market share in the music streaming market as of 2017. (Spotify did not respond to MarketWatch’s request for comment.)
Appearing on high-profile playlists on Spotify can make or break a new artist’s career. In its IPO filing earlier this year, Spotify attributed the breakout success of New Zealander singer Lorde (and her single “Royals,” in particular) to her appearance on the “Hipster International” playlist maintained by Napster co-founder and former Facebook FB, +1.26% president Sean Parker.
But not all playlists are created equally — and the most popular ones on Spotify are curated by the streaming service itself rather than by individual listeners. Spotify-created lists attract roughly three-quarters of all the followers of the top 1,000 tracks on the platform.
Also see: The Spotify IPO filing includes a giant warning sign
Certain playlists can be critical in raising the profile of an artist or song. For instance, if a song is added to the Today’s Top Hits playlist, which had 18.5 million followers during the research period, it will receive roughly 20 million more streams on average.
That boost equates to serious monetary gains. The 20 million additional streams translate to somewhere between $116,000 and $163,000 in added revenue for the musician. And the Today’s Top Hits playlist isn’t the only one of its kind. Being the top song on the New Music Fridays list will lead to receiving 14 million more streams roughly, which adds up to a financial gain of between $84,000 and $117,000.
For instance, Kane Brown’s single, “What Ifs,” saw its number of followers increase from 11.6 million to 29.2 million after it was added to Today’s Top Hits playlist in October 2017. It maintained that following for the next month that it appeared on the playlist — but the day the song was dropped from the list its following dropped to 10.8 million accounts. And as other playlists de-listed the song, its following reduced even further.
The popular New Music Friday lists that Spotify produces had diverse representation — more than half of the tracks are from independent labels or artists, and U.S.-made music only accounts for a third of the songs. But otherwise the service’s most popular playlists, including lists produced by Spotify, are dominated by major labels like Universal Music Group VIV, -0.64% Sony Music Entertainment SNE, -1.53% and Warner Music Group T, -2.90%

For these other lists, though independent record labels account for just under half of the songs, they only garner about a quarter of the streams.
However, an artist being included on an official Spotify playlist doesn’t always correspond to how often people listen to their music. The working paper found that being included on a popular Spotify playlist was not correlated with a noted uptick in downloads on iTunes.
Spotify announced last month that it was removing R. Kelly from its in-house playlists in light of multiple accusations of sexual abuse against the singer (who is not currently facing any criminal charges). Through a statement issued by his management team last month, R. Kelly denied the allegations .
But the move made little impact on how many people streamed his music. In fact there was even a slight increase, the Associated Press reported . More from MarketWatch
